correctness.rationale: On the positive unit sphere, the objective is a degree-p homogeneous quotient. Every boundary face is strictly suboptimal: B=0 gives zero, moving A from zero gains order epsilon^(p-1) versus epsilon^p in the denominator, and moving C from zero gains order epsilon versus epsilon^p. The interior Lagrange equations force the quotient lambda=(p-1)a/(pA), C^(p-1)=bA/((p-1)a), and A^p+(p-1)(b/a)AC=p-1. The substitution u=A^(p/(p-1)) gives a strictly monotone equation with precisely one positive solution. Compactness forces this solution to be globally maximizing. Phase rigidity follows from equality in the complex triangle inequality. The full argument, including p near 1 and real signs, is reconstructed in RESULT.md. CHECK.py is supplementary; its 60000 sampled comparisons cannot serve as proof.

originality.rationale: The public 2010 Lp paper computes the single-link (two-dimensional) rank-one shift value and general positive-operator lower bounds; those give no exact coupled two-link numerical radius. The 2015 weighted-shift paper uses Hilbert-space Hermitian spectral theory, with only the p=2 value on the target family. The 2012 permutation article likewise explicitly assumes complex Hilbert space. Available Hardy-space and semi-inner-product numerical-range examples do not imply the formula. Search and primary-text comparisons leave bounded coverage risks but no decisive dominating theorem.

The complete body of the 2011 Hardy-space and 2012 semi-inner-product publications was not obtained.

value.rationale: A positive two-link nilpotent path is the first weighted shift where adjacent norming-functional products genuinely interact, beyond the classical rank-one shift. The theorem computes a natural sharp operator invariant for all positive edge weights and all real Banach exponents (and both scalar fields), with unique magnitude profile and complete equality-case phases. The monotone one-variable root makes the exact constant usable in non-Hilbert numerical-radius benchmarks; its p=4 value is not the Hilbert spectral answer. It is neither an arbitrary parameter slice nor a restatement of the general positive-operator lower bound.
